_about: In-game help (GDD 5 'Help'). 'screens' = one entry per screen or screen state, opened by that screen's '?' button; 'topics' = ideas used on several screens, opened from a section's 'see' list (a 'See also' button). Raise an entry's 'version' when its text changes in a meaningful way: the '?' shows its 'new' dot again. Sections: a heading and at most ~50 words of plain text. No hidden numbers (injury proneness, strain, formulas). Each new feature adds or updates its entry here (CLAUDE.md).

sections.heading: Season goals
sections.text: Under the Today card: the three goals you and your coach set for the season, with how you stand. ✓ means met, ✗ missed. With none yet, you can ask your coach for goals.

sections.heading: Mind
sections.text: Beside or under the goals: your confidence, motivation and stress, each a word with an arrow when it rose or fell since last week. Tap one to see what it does now, what moved it lately, what is pulling it and what helps.

sections.heading: Playing the days
sections.text: Next day plays one day. Play week plays on to Sunday night, but it stops early when something needs you: a race, a new injury, a warning sign or your coach's Sunday talk. The game saves itself after every day.

sections.heading: Messages
sections.text: A message from your coach or someone else shows at the top of the Today card, with a dot when it is new or waits for your answer. Tap it to open the conversation in the People tab.

sections.heading: The week strip
sections.text: Monday to Sunday of this week; tap a day to see or change it. Each mark is a session: blue Easy, grey Normal, red Hard. RACE is a meet you entered, a small dot means you changed that day, and played days are dimmed.

sections.heading: School on the strip
sections.text: A day shaded teal is a school break or holiday. A violet T marks a day with a test (a number when there are several). Tap the day to see it as morning, school, training and evening.

sections.heading: ! and + on a day
sections.text: A round ! means you were sore that day; its colour says how sore. A + means an injury or illness limited the day; its colour says how serious it is. A small speech bubble means someone wrote to you that day: filled while it is new.

sections.heading: Your coach's initial
sections.text: A round letter in your coach's colour means he changed that day. Tap the day to see why, and to veto it if you disagree.

sections.heading: How you feel
sections.text: Your fatigue: Fresh, Normal, Tired or Exhausted. Training adds to it and rest takes it away. When you are tired, sessions train you less and races go slower.

sections.heading: Race form
sections.text: How you would race if the race were today. It is not about fitness: it is about being sharp and fresh on the day.

sections.heading: Warning signs
sections.text: Body areas that feel sore after training, worst first. Tap one to see why it is sore and what helps. "A bit sore" is the early warning.

sections.heading: Injury and illness
sections.text: What you have now, what you are allowed to do, and when you are expected back. Tap it for a plain explanation.

sections.heading: Attributes
sections.text: Your abilities on a scale of 1 to 20. Training changes them on Sunday nights; growing up helps for a few years around your growth spurt. As for real runners, yearly gains shrink from about 16 (girls 15) as you near your limit. Untrained abilities fade slowly. Arrows show recent rises and falls; tap one to see what it does.

sections.heading: Progress by month
sections.text: The button under your body facts opens the Progress page: a record of your attributes and best time at the end of every month, so you can see how fast you are really improving.

sections.heading: Saving
sections.text: Besides the automatic save, the Save button makes an extra copy you can load later from the main menu. On a computer, Ctrl+S does the same.

sections.heading: What a season plan is
sections.text: Your club coach's training year, November to October, split into phases that build up to your target meets. Every week's training comes from the phase it is in, so you don't have to plan each week yourself.

sections.heading: The coach's three plans
sections.text: Steady, Balanced and Ambitious differ in how much you train. ★ is the plan your coach would pick for you now. More training brings more progress but more risk: Ambitious only pays off if you back off when your body warns you. Change plan shows the three side by side.

sections.heading: Plans grow with you
sections.text: The coach's plans are made for your age group: 14–15, 16–17, 18–19 and adults. Each step adds training: more easy running, a second speed session, strength twice a week, and as an adult your first double days. The season you move up, the plan cards say what is new.

sections.heading: Next season
sections.text: Three weeks before a new season your coach offers the three plans again. Until the season starts, the Next season box here lets you choose or change. If you don't choose, the season starts on the coach's ★ plan, and you're entered in its target meets.

sections.heading: Easing back in
sections.text: After two weeks or more without running, your coach suggests a few easier weeks before your full plan. While they run, a box at the top shows the weeks, and you can stop them early.

sections.heading: The phases
sections.text: General base builds your engine in winter. Indoor specific sharpens you for the indoor target. Spring base builds again before summer. Pre-competition and race season are for racing. Transition is a few easy weeks of rest, and autumn general starts the new year gently. Tap a phase to see or change it.

sections.heading: Lighter weeks and easing in
sections.text: In the base phases every fourth week is lighter, so your body can catch up. A new phase doesn't start all at once: its sessions come in a day at a time over the first weeks.

sections.heading: Target meets ◆
sections.text: Up to three a season. Your plan builds up to them, and the last ten days before each one are a taper so you arrive fresh and sharp.

sections.heading: Body strain
sections.text: Under this week's plan: how much you train compared with your usual weeks, and how risky the plan is for your body right now.

sections.heading: This week
sections.text: The list shows the week as it is right now, the same days as the week strip: races, days already played, and days you, your coach or an injury changed. The phase's own plan is behind it, and the coach's reason for a day is under it.

sections.heading: Over the week strip
sections.text: The line above the week strip shows the phase and week you are in, how many days are left before a target, or the week of easing back in.

sections.heading: One repeating week
sections.text: The switch at the top lets you plan one week yourself instead, repeated every week. Your season plan is kept, and you can switch back at any time.

sections.heading: Ask your coach
sections.text: Under this week's plan, ask your coach what he thinks of the plan from next week on: changed against his, or as it is against an easier week.

sections.heading: Mental training
sections.text: Above the standing orders: imagery, relaxation and self-talk, one short session of each a week if you switch it on. No body strain. Self-talk has a cue word that shows on your race cards.

sections.heading: School life
sections.text: Above the standing orders: your study effort and your free time. They change how heavy your school days are and how your grades go, never what you train. The School page in the People tab has the grades.

sections.heading: Standing orders
sections.text: At the bottom: what Play week stops for (Important only, or Every moment), whether your coach may change your days, from grade 9 on how your lukio courses are planned (you every period, or the counsellor), and the rules you made from repeated answers, each with Remove.

sections.heading: The phase's week
sections.text: This week repeats through the whole phase, with the season's rules on top (lighter weeks, easing in, the easy day before a race, the taper). Change sessions and Easy / Normal / Hard here as in a repeating week.

sections.heading: Ask your coach
sections.text: Under the week, ask your coach about it: your changed week against his, or his own week against an easier one. For a later phase he judges it from where your body will be by then.

sections.heading: Your changes
sections.text: A phase you changed is marked "your changes". Back to coach's puts the coach's week back.

sections.heading: Lighter weeks
sections.text: Switch the lighter weeks on or off for this phase. A lighter week makes every day one step easier.

sections.heading: Easing in
sections.text: How many weeks the phase takes to blend in from the phase before it. Fewer is a quicker change, more is gentler on the body.

sections.heading: When it runs
sections.text: Earlier and Later move the start or the end by a week; moving an end moves the next phase's start too. Weeks that have already begun can't move, so this week never changes under you.

sections.heading: Body strain of a later phase
sections.text: For a phase that hasn't started yet, the load and risk are worked out as if you follow your plan until then: they show what switching into this phase will feel like.

sections.heading: Easing back in
sections.text: After two weeks or more without running, your coach can put a few easier weeks over your plan. While they run, a box at the top shows them, and you can stop them early.

sections.heading: Your week
sections.text: You plan one week and it repeats every week until you change it. Up to two sessions a day; an empty day is a rest day. To change only one day of this week, tap it in the week strip.

sections.heading: Easy, Normal, Hard
sections.text: How hard you do the day's sessions. Hard trains you a bit more but tires you and strains your body much more. Easy keeps most of the training effect for much less strain, which makes it a good way to train more without getting hurt.

sections.heading: Coach's plan and Clear week
sections.text: Coach's plan puts back the starter week your club coach suggests. Clear week empties every day so you can start from scratch.

sections.heading: Ask your coach
sections.text: Under the buttons, ask your coach about your week: changed against his starter week, or his own week against an easier one.

sections.heading: The summary
sections.text: Weekly load, the fatigue you can expect after a few weeks of this plan, what it trains, and the body strain.

sections.heading: Sessions and seasons
sections.text: Outdoor tracks are closed from November to April. Without an indoor track, track sessions are done on roads and work less well. Skiing is possible from December to March. The list at the bottom says what each session trains.

sections.heading: Back to the season plan
sections.text: The switch at the top takes you back to your coach's season plan, with your earlier changes to it.

sections.heading: The same week for months
sections.text: A week that never changes wears your motivation down after about two months, and low motivation trains you a little less. Changing the week now and then keeps it fresh.

sections.heading: Mental training
sections.text: Above the standing orders: imagery, relaxation and self-talk, one short session of each a week if you switch it on. No body strain. Self-talk has a cue word that shows on your race cards.

sections.heading: School life
sections.text: Above the standing orders: your study effort and your free time. They change how heavy your school days are and how your grades go, never what you train. The School page in the People tab has the grades.

sections.heading: Standing orders
sections.text: At the very bottom: what Play week stops for (Important only, or Every moment), whether your coach may change your days, from grade 9 on how your lukio courses are planned (you every period, or the counsellor), and the rules you made from repeated answers, each with Remove.

sections.heading: School on the Calendar
sections.text: Between the meets: school breaks (teal), busy test weeks (violet) and the Pajulahti camp weeks for grades 7-9, information only for now. Grade 9 adds the joint application's dates; lukio adds each period's exam week, your matriculation sessions and their registration deadlines (violet).

sections.heading: Your coach suggests
sections.text: A meet marked COACH SUGGESTS is one he thinks worth racing, with his reason. Enter it, or No thanks: he won't suggest it again. He also suggests making a meet a target. He never enters you himself.

sections.heading: Entering a meet
sections.text: Tap Enter to race a meet. On race day the race replaces that day's training. Tap Entered ✓ again to withdraw.

sections.heading: ★ and ◆
sections.text: ★ means your coach suggests the meet. ◆ marks one of your season's target meets; Make target turns a meet into one (at most three a season).

sections.heading: Qualifying times
sections.text: Championships have a qualifying time for your age class. The meet says whether you have it. You may still enter one event without it. The best runners of your age class usually enter, so a championship field is about as big as the real one, often 10 to 30.

sections.heading: The seasons
sections.text: Indoor meets run from December to March, outdoor meets from May to September. "Estimated" dates are believable guesses for meets whose real dates aren't out yet. Club meets have adult classes too. Senior meets are shown, but you follow them from home for now.

sections.heading: What this list is
sections.text: Everyone's best 800 m time of the calendar year in your age class: you and your rivals, ranked fastest first. It fills up as the season goes on, because rivals only appear once they have raced this year.

sections.heading: You
sections.text: The YOU box at the top gives your place, your season best and the gap to the runner just ahead. Your row in the list is highlighted and marked (you).

sections.heading: Season bests
sections.text: Indoor and outdoor times count together, as in real result lists. The top 25 are shown, and you always are.

sections.heading: Your rivals
sections.text: Your rivals train and race on their own, so the list fills up as the season goes on. Like real runners they improve fast at 14 and 15, then more slowly every year, and most of them level off. They get injured too and miss races now and then.

sections.heading: This week
sections.text: A short summary of the week so far: days played, sessions, training load, how tired you are, races and health. Tap Day by day to open every day: what you did, your fatigue, sore areas, injuries and anything that happened. School days show their tests and scores.

sections.heading: Last week
sections.text: Sessions, training load and how your fatigue went, plus races, health and the season plan line. Attributes are shown when one moved a whole point: progress is added on Sunday night and builds up slowly. The days of that week are folded under Day by day.

sections.heading: The people around you
sections.text: Your coach, your training group, your family, your friends from school and, once you have raced someone a few times, your rivals. A number or a dot means something is new or waits for your answer. Tap a row to open the conversation.

sections.heading: Who they are
sections.text: At the top of a thread: who the people are and how you get on with each (Close, Good, Fine, Cool, Strained). Your family's attitude comes from your story: some are proud, some think grades come first. Your answers slowly change both.

sections.heading: What an answer changes
sections.text: Never your training. An answer can move your moods, how someone feels about you, give you a late night (a heavier next day) or nudge your schoolwork. The card after an answer says what changed.

sections.heading: School
sections.text: The School row opens your grades, tests and report cards, the two school settings, the joint application and the school after grade 9. Your teachers' messages are at the top of that page.

sections.heading: Other coaches
sections.text: Other coaches write to you in their own thread: answers when you ask one to coach you, and offers after a breakthrough. At a sports lukio the school's morning-practice coach writes in your first week. Find a coach shows every coach you can see now.

sections.heading: Answering
sections.text: Tap an answer. The line under each button says what it may cost, like "he will remember". A message you leave unanswered passes after a day or two as "You didn't answer", and the other person notices a little. The newest talk is on top.

sections.heading: The Sunday talk
sections.text: Every Sunday evening your coach looks back at the week and ahead at the next one: the phase, the hard sessions and why, and one thing to focus on. It always stops Play week. A talk may end with a question. After a race he writes to you that evening.

sections.heading: Coach profile
sections.text: Who your coach is, the character, how well you fit and how much you trust each other. The skills are a range that narrows week by week and is exact after eight weeks together. Below them is the training group.

sections.heading: Settings
sections.text: What Play week stops for, and your saved rules, are at the bottom of the Training tab.

sections.heading: What school does
sections.text: School changes how heavy your days are and how your grades go. It never changes what you train. A normal school week at Normal study effort and Normal free time is just your normal game.

sections.heading: Messages from school
sections.text: Your class teacher, PE teacher and study counsellor write at the top of this page: tests, the school's cross-country run, the work-experience week, the application. Some answers nudge your grades a little or cost you a late night.

sections.heading: Study effort
sections.text: Light, Normal or Heavy. Heavy lifts your grades but makes school days heavier: more tiredness and more colds. Light does the opposite. The same two settings are in the Training tab.

sections.heading: Free time
sections.text: Little, Normal or Lots. Lots of free time with friends lifts your motivation but means late nights on school days. Little means more rest, but life gets dull.

sections.heading: Focus subjects
sections.text: Pick up to two subjects to push. They rise faster while the others slip a little. Change them any time: grades move slowly, so switching back and forth gains nothing.

sections.heading: Grades and tests
sections.text: Each subject shows where you stand, written like a test: 8, 8+, 8½, 9-. Tap one for its latest tests. A week with more than two tests is a busy test week: heavier and more stressful.

sections.heading: Report cards
sections.text: In grades 8 and 9 you get a report card on the last school day before Christmas and at the end of the school year. Play stops to show it, and you choose how to handle the next term. Your family reacts the next evening. In lukio each period has its results instead.

sections.heading: Tests and a race
sections.text: When you have a race in a busy test week, a test on the race day itself, or a matriculation exam that week, play stops once. Race and risk the grades, study and scratch, or race and study on the bus: each has a price. Exam weeks nearly always count as busy.

sections.heading: Holidays
sections.text: Breaks and the summer are lighter: you recover a little faster and feel less stressed. The week strip shades those days and the Calendar lists them. Pajulahti camp weeks are shown there too.

sections.heading: The joint application
sections.text: In grade 9 you apply for upper secondary school: up to seven wishes in order, in February-March. A sports lukio counts your grades (0-10 points), your 800 m results (0-5) and its own test (0-5). Add schools, tap Info, reorder. Nothing chosen means your own town's lukio.

sections.heading: Test day and results
sections.text: In May the sports lukiot that invited you test you: a physical test and an interview, with three choices that count. In June you get the results: the first wish that accepts you is your place. If none does, you can pick a general lukio, a vocational school or a TUVA year (a preparatory year for raising grades).

sections.heading: After grade 9
sections.text: A lukio has five periods a year; each ends with an exam week, heavy on school life. A sports lukio has morning practice: a second session on those days costs no extra school load. A vocational school has no grades or exam weeks here.

sections.heading: Lukio courses
sections.text: Lukio is 75 courses. The study counsellor plans them over your periods; each period starts with a stop where you can change its courses and ends with your grades. More courses in a period make its school days heavier.

sections.heading: Matriculation exams
sections.text: At the end of lukio you take the matriculation exams on their real dates: Finnish and at least four more. You choose them and their sessions; each session is locked when its registration closes.

sections.heading: Moving
sections.text: A school in another town means moving there on 1 August. You keep racing for your club, but your old coach is far away and you may want a coach near the new school. The coaches there appear in Find a coach.

sections.heading: Who you can get
sections.text: At 14 and 15: your club's coaches and a parent who competed in athletics. From 16, or once you reach the TF-juniorit standard: other clubs in your town, coaches in your region, national coaches and remote coaches. An athletics-centre town has more.

sections.heading: Coaches choose too
sections.text: A coach may want a time from you first, or have no place this season. Club fees always fit; a personal coach must fit your family's monthly budget.

sections.heading: Offers
sections.text: Coaches also write to you themselves, when they see a reason: a talent they think is wasted, a slump, fast progress, a best that reaches their group. An offer is only as good as the coach: a poor judge can misread you or promise too much. Nothing changes unless you start with the coach. Switch offers off on this page.

sections.heading: Offers under 18
sections.text: A coach does not write to an athlete under 18. He calls a parent, who tells you in the family thread. His offer waits on his page here, with the cost and the place kept for 30 days. "Not now" keeps him quiet for half a year.

sections.heading: Finding out more
sections.text: Skills show as ranges. Look at the athletes' results, ask around (a teammate answers) or visit a session (that day becomes an easy run, or a rest day if it means travel). Eight weeks together make every skill exact.

sections.heading: Changing coach
sections.text: Ask to be coached; if the answer is yes, start on the next Monday. Your old coach, the group and the club will notice. A new coach starts as New trust, with a new group.

sections.heading: When a coach ends it
sections.text: Only after weeks of Strained trust and two warning talks. Answering them well brings trust back. If it still ends, you choose your next coach from those who would take you.

moment.title: A message that stops the week

sections.heading: Goals and suggestions
sections.text: Your coach also writes about your season goals, when one is met or the season is looked back on, and when he suggests a meet to race or a target. Nothing is decided without you.

sections.heading: Why it stops
sections.text: Your coach's Sunday talk always stops Play week. Other messages stop it when your answer really matters: a party the night before a race, the cottage week, your family on your report card. About one a week. Pick an answer to carry on.

sections.heading: Your coach suggests a change
sections.text: He wants to change a coming day, or advises you to scratch from a race. OK lets him. Veto keeps your plan: a reason costs nothing, but many vetoes without one cost a little trust.

sections.heading: The answers
sections.text: The line under each button says what it may cost, like "he will remember". A talk without a question just needs "Thanks, coach".

sections.heading: Later
sections.text: The whole conversation stays in the People tab. What Play week stops for is a setting at the bottom of the Training tab.

sections.heading: Season goals
sections.text: At the top: this season's goals with how you stand, and a line for each earlier season. A goal is ✓ when met and ✗ when missed.

sections.heading: The record
sections.text: A snapshot of all your attributes, your 800 m ability and your personal best, taken when your career started and at the end of every month. It is saved with your career. An older save starts its record the day you first load it.

sections.heading: Since the start
sections.text: The box at the top compares the first record with now: how much your ability and best time improved and which attributes grew most.

sections.heading: A month
sections.text: Tap a record to open it: every attribute with its value and how much it changed since the record before (a dash means hardly at all). Races that month are listed under the title with the best time.

sections.heading: The day at school
sections.text: At the top: your day in four blocks (morning, school, training, evening) and how heavy the day is for you at school. Holidays are lighter. Tests in a busy week, late nights and two practices on a school day are heavier.

sections.heading: This week only
sections.text: Changes here are for this one day of this week. Days already played and race days can't be changed. To change every week, use the Training tab.

sections.heading: Your coach says
sections.text: Under the sessions your coach tells you why you do the day. A coach who explains a lot gives the reason; a quiet one just says what to do. His voice follows his character.

sections.heading: Sessions
sections.text: Swap a session, remove it, add a second one (two at most) or make the day a rest day. A greyed-out session isn't possible this time of year, or with your injury; the reason is in its name.

sections.heading: Easy, Normal, Hard
sections.text: How hard you do the day. The day's load is shown next to what your plan has. Hard trains a bit more but strains the body much more.

sections.heading: Back to plan
sections.text: A changed day says who changed it. Back to plan returns the day to your plan. The "Season plan" line says why the day looks as it does: a lighter week, easing in, an easy day before a race, the taper or easing back in after a layoff.

sections.heading: Changed by your coach
sections.text: A day your coach changed shows his reason at the top. Veto puts your plan back; then pick why. A reason costs nothing.

sections.heading: Ask your coach
sections.text: At the bottom, ask your coach about the day as it stands, or about a race: race it or scratch? His answer shows right there.

sections.heading: Injury limits
sections.text: An injury or illness takes out what you shouldn't do. With a minor problem you can train through it, but it can make it worse and take longer to heal. "Locked" means it isn't allowed at all.

sections.heading: Race day
sections.text: On a race day you see the meet and your race form. If you are injured or ill, you can scratch (not start), and your coach may advise you to. A played day only shows what you did.

sections.heading: Your coach suggests
sections.text: A suggested plan and kick plan, in his own words. Use his plan fills in the choices below; you can still change them. His view is only as good as his race reading, and his character tilts it: a hard coach likes the front, a calm one waits, a warm one plays safe.

sections.heading: The field
sections.text: The runners in your race (your section or heat at a championship), fastest personal best first, with this year's best (SB). Once you have raced a runner twice you also see how they run: Front runner, Pack runner, Kicker or Surger.

sections.heading: Sections and heats
sections.text: Finnish championships run the 800 m in sections: the fastest runners in the last one, places and medals by time across all sections. PLACES says about what a medal and the top 8 will need. Senior and international meets have heats: the first few go through (Q), then the fastest of the rest (q).

sections.heading: You
sections.text: How you feel today, your race form, and a warning if you would race injured or ill.

sections.heading: Race plan
sections.text: The plan is where you want to run. Lead: set the pace, no traffic, but no shelter from the wind. Sit in the pack: run behind others near the front and save energy. Wait at the back: save the most for a late kick, at the risk of getting boxed in or left behind.

sections.heading: Kick plan
sections.text: For a Quick result only: the distance at which your athlete starts the kick. Natural means where their body suits. An earlier start than your body suits looks brave but dies before the line. When you watch the race, you decide the kick yourself.

sections.heading: Quick result or Watch and decide
sections.text: Quick result runs the race at once with your plan and your kick plan, and your athlete makes the decisions as well as their race tactics allow. Watch and decide shows the race, stops for your decisions and gives you the action bar. If you are injured, you can still scratch before the first round.

sections.heading: The track
sections.text: Each dot is a runner; yours is highlighted. The buttons at the top change the speed: 1x is real time. Outdoors the race runs in lanes until the first bend is over, indoors until the second, then everyone cuts in. In a section or heat, the line under the clock says about what time you need.

sections.heading: Pause
sections.text: The pause button next to 1x, 2x and 4x (on a PC also the Space bar) stops the race, so you can look at the track and the positions. The action bar still works: your command is given at once and the race acts on it when you run on. Tap it again to go on.

sections.heading: Slowing down
sections.text: At 2x or 4x the race drops to 1x for a few seconds when something happens close to you: a rival kicks or makes a move, someone stumbles or falls, or you get boxed in. A note under the clock says what, then the speed goes back.

sections.heading: Your energy
sections.text: Every runner has a pace they can hold and a reserve for anything faster. Running behind someone saves a little. Going faster than your own even pace burns the reserve quickly: spend it too early and you tie up in the finish.

sections.heading: Feeling
sections.text: The word under the clock says how much you have left, as you feel it: Comfortable, Working, Hurting or Empty. Your race tactics decide how well you judge it, so it can be wrong. Being tired before the race makes it worse.

sections.heading: The action bar
sections.text: Always there; the race does not stop. Push, Hold and Ease set your pace until you kick. Move out takes you wide for a few seconds to go past. Kick now starts your kick at any distance, even in the last 100 m: tap it twice within two seconds, so a slip of the thumb does not.

sections.heading: Your kick
sections.text: At your kick point a card asks when you go. Kick now starts it. Wait, I'll call it means nothing starts the kick for you: you press Kick now when you want to go. The note under the clock says YOUR CALL. If you never press it, you never kick.

sections.heading: In the pack
sections.text: Rivals make moves: a surge, or a kick for home. A mover who has the strength presses on and gets away from those who let it go; one who hasn't is caught. Going with a move costs energy: worth it against an equal, rarely against someone clearly stronger.

sections.heading: Boxed in and falls
sections.text: Stuck on the inside behind a runner, with one on your shoulder, you're boxed in. Someone right on your shoulder: wait, a gap usually comes soon (rarely on a bend). Room on your outside: ease off and step out, or push through near the line. Tight bunches clip heels: stumbles, now and then a fall.

sections.heading: Decisions
sections.text: The race pauses when something really happens: after the break, at the bell, a rival's move, being boxed in, losing contact, a slow pace, your own kick, the home straight, after a fall. If your coach can see you, the coach shouts what to do. The advice is usually right, not always.

sections.heading: The card
sections.text: A decision card sits beside the track (on a phone, in a sheet below it), so you can see what is happening while you choose. The race waits until you answer, and the action bar is dimmed meanwhile.

sections.heading: Your word
sections.text: With self-talk in your mental training (Training tab), the cue word you picked shows on every card: the word you say to yourself when it hurts.

sections.heading: Commentary
sections.text: A stadium announcer calls small meets; at championships a commentator and an expert explain what you may miss: moves that get away, kicks that die, boxes, heat runners easing off. Key moments flash over the top of the track. The newest line is also under the track (a phone: the ticker; tap it for the whole log, the race waits).

sections.heading: Your coach
sections.text: Your coach sits in the stands: outdoors by the 200 m start (the diamond), indoors at the hall rail. He speaks only about what he can see: your splits as you pass him, the cards, your kick. Each coach has a personality: calm, hard, warm or tactical. About ten seconds after a choice you hear how it is working out.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Your place and time. PB marks a personal best and SB the best time of the year, for you and for the others in every list. The time counts in the season rankings.

sections.heading: Race story
sections.text: Your times at 200, 400 and 600 m and the finish with your place at each, next to the winner's (or the runner-up's when you won), the key moments of the race and what your coach thinks of it. The coach judges your time against your own level too: a personal best is never a bad race.

sections.heading: Sections
sections.text: After sections you see everyone by time across all of them (S2 = section 2): that is the official result. Your section's own list comes below it, then the other sections. Winning a slow section can still be 10th overall.

sections.heading: DNF and DQ
sections.text: DNF: did not finish, after a bad fall. DQ: disqualified for obstruction, after pushing your way out of a box. Neither counts for a personal best or the rankings. A fall can leave you with grazes or a bruise, rarely a sprained ankle.

sections.heading: Heats and final
sections.text: Senior and international meets have heats; after yours you see every heat's result, yours first. Q = through on place, q = through on time: the fastest of the rest. How many go through follows the World Athletics table; a big field adds semi-finals. Runners safely through ease off before the line.

sections.heading: Who you are
sections.text: Your name, gender, hometown and club. You start as a 14-year-old in November 2026.

sections.heading: Main event
sections.text: The event you train for and race. The 800 m is playable now; more events come later.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Your answers shape your starting abilities: every answer has strengths and weaknesses. Where you train also decides whether you have an indoor track in winter.

sections.heading: Your points
sections.text: Everyone gets 6 points; every bit of organised training in your story adds more, up to 16. At most +3 on any one ability. More training means a stronger start but slower growth: a beginner improves much faster in the first two years and often catches up by 16 or 17.

sections.heading: What counts for the 800 m
sections.text: The dots show how much an ability counts for your 800 m time. The coach's guess updates as you spend. Not sure? Let the coach spread them. Some things about your talent stay hidden and show over the years.

sections.heading: A diagnosis
sections.text: A niggle lets you train with limits, an injury stops running for a while, a serious injury means weeks out. Expected time is a range: it moves later if you train through it. The limits are already in your week.

sections.heading: Locked or "may get worse"
sections.text: Locked means you can't train or race against the limits. Otherwise you may, but it strains the area more and can turn into something worse.

sections.heading: A soreness warning
sections.text: An area just turned sore. Keep going trains as planned. Take it easy makes today Easy. A rest day gives the body the most time. Before a race, you choose between racing and scratching.

sections.heading: Choosing a plan
sections.text: Steady, Balanced and Ambitious are the same training year with more or less work. Tap a card to see it chosen, then press Use. ★ is the plan your coach would pick for you now, from your durability, professionalism and recent injuries.

sections.heading: Your age group
sections.text: The line above the cards says which age group the plans are for. When you move up a group, it also says what the coach adds: as you grow older, the same plan name means more training.

sections.heading: What the cards say
sections.text: Weekly load is the season's average week. The risk word is what most weeks of the plan read for an athlete like you. More load brings more progress, but only if you listen to your body.

sections.heading: Decide later
sections.text: Nothing is lost: you can choose in the Training tab until the season starts. If you never choose, the season runs on the ★ plan. Choosing never removes your target meets.

sections.heading: Why the coach suggests it
sections.text: While you weren't running, your body lost some of what it was used to. Your old plan is now a big jump, and big jumps are when injuries happen. The risk line shows what your plan would mean with and without easing back in.

sections.heading: The weeks
sections.text: The first week is one easy session a day, with no hard or fast running. Then one session a day at Normal with one hard session kept. A long break ends with a lighter week. Your races stay as they are.

sections.heading: Accept or No thanks
sections.text: Accept puts the weeks over your plan from tomorrow; you can stop them early in the Training tab or the day editor. No thanks keeps your plan as it is.

sections.heading: Three goals
sections.text: With his plan for a season your coach offers three goals: a time you run, a milestone (a real limit or a place at a meet) and a habit (sessions you do, warnings you respect, races you run). You pick the level of each.

sections.heading: Choosing a level
sections.text: The arrows step through the levels, from Safe to Dream. The star marks the level he would pick; it follows how demanding he is. The words say how likely it is, in his eyes.

sections.heading: His estimate
sections.text: He plays your plan forward and guesses what you can run at the season's peak. A coach who judges you well sets goals that fit. A poor judge may set goals that are too easy or too hard, and you won't see it until the season shows.

sections.heading: Real limits
sections.text: A milestone can be a real limit of the Finnish Athletics Federation: the SM limit, the Team Finland criteria or the Kalevan kisat limit.

sections.heading: When a goal is met
sections.text: It counts as soon as you reach it: he writes to you and your trust in him grows, a little more if you chose a level above his. What is still open is settled when the season ends.

sections.heading: When it is missed
sections.text: A missed goal never costs you trust. He looks back with you after the meet or at the season's end. What you answer tells him how to set next season's goals: the same, higher or lower.

sections.heading: Where you see them
sections.text: On the Overview and the Progress page, with how you stand. If you decided later, ask your coach for goals on the Overview.

sections.heading: What this is
sections.text: A menu for testing the game, only in a test build (the game run from the Godot editor). A finished game does not show it. Nothing here counts as real play.

sections.heading: Watch a test race
sections.text: Pick indoor or outdoor, sections or heats, and a meet level, then Start test race. A separate test career is played to such a race and the race opens. Your own saves are never touched and the test career is never saved.

sections.heading: The level
sections.text: The meet's level decides who commentates: a stadium announcer at local and district meets, one commentator at a national championship, a commentator and an expert at international youth meets and on TV.

sections.heading: Jump the career forward
sections.text: Plays the career you have open to the next race day or to a date. The days are played for real and the game is saved once at the end. The jump stops early at a race or when something needs your answer.

sections.heading: Test moments
sections.text: Placeholder messages from your coach and training group. Open a career (Open my latest save), switch them On, then Go to the career and play. Important ones stop Play week as a panel; the rest wait and are listed here. Every moment makes all of them stop.

sections.heading: Back to your own career
sections.text: After a test race, press Main menu and then Continue or Load. A test career shows TEST CAREER at the top and cannot be saved.

sections.heading: Same town
sections.text: You train with the coach and the group every day: the full coaching.

sections.heading: Same region
sections.text: You train together about two days a week and follow the plan on the others. The coach sees less of you, so technique and load management are a little weaker, and race advice is weaker at meets the coach does not come to.

sections.heading: Far away
sections.text: A remote coach: the plan comes by message, a visit about once a month and the national meets together. Technique, load management and race reading at the other meets suffer more. Moving to a centre town comes with the sports school, later.

sections.heading: Tired legs
sections.text: Fatigue is how tired your whole body is, from 0 to 100: Fresh, Normal, Tired, Exhausted. Every session adds to it, and some of it fades every day, more on rest days.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: When you are tired, sessions train you less, races are slower and illnesses come more easily. Being a bit tired in heavy training weeks is normal; staying Tired for weeks is not.

sections.heading: Not the same as soreness
sections.text: Fatigue is the whole body and goes away in days. Soreness is one body area under strain, and it is the warning before an injury.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.text: Each body area (shins, feet, knees, heels, hamstrings, calves) takes strain from training. Strain shows as soreness: a bit sore, sore, painful.

sections.heading: The early warning
sections.text: "A bit sore" is when to listen: an easy day or a rest day now usually stops it from turning into an injury. Training on through "sore" and "painful" is how most injuries start.

sections.heading: What makes it worse
sections.text: Hard days, tired legs, sudden jumps in training, hard winter roads, a growth spurt and an old injury in the same place.

sections.heading: Kinds
sections.text: A niggle is a small problem you can train with. An injury means no running for a while, then easy running. A serious injury means weeks to months out. A cold allows easy training; with a fever you rest.

sections.heading: While you are out
sections.text: Banned sessions are swapped for ones that are allowed, such as pool running or the bike, which keep much of your fitness. Your abilities don't drop for good; you lose time.

sections.heading: Training through it
sections.text: With a minor problem you may ignore the limits, but each day of it adds healing time and can turn the problem into something worse.

sections.heading: Coming back
sections.text: After time off, your body is no longer used to full training. Jumping straight back into your old plan is itself a big risk: build up again. After two weeks or more without running, your coach offers a few weeks of easing back in.

sections.heading: What it shows
sections.text: How much this plan's week trains you compared with your average week over the last four weeks. 100 % is your usual.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Your body gets used to the training it is given. A gradual build-up is safe; a sudden jump (well above 120 %) is when injuries happen. Right after a break even a normal week is a big jump.

sections.heading: What it shows
sections.text: How likely this plan is to give you an overuse injury in the next few weeks, given what your body is used to now: Low, Moderate or High.

sections.heading: How to use it
sections.text: It is a guide, not a promise: bodies differ, and bad luck happens. To lower it, add Easy days or a rest day, take out a hard session, or build up over a few weeks.

sections.heading: What it means
sections.text: How fast you would race today compared with a normal day: Peaking, Sharp, OK, Rusty, or Tired. It changes your race time by a little, often enough to win or lose a place.

sections.heading: Sharpness
sections.text: Race-like work keeps you sharp: 800 m intervals, the club session, speed and strides, and races. It fades within a week or two without them.

sections.heading: Freshness
sections.text: Low fatigue on race day. A few lighter days before a race make you fresh; a taper gives you both and is how you peak.

sections.heading: Your choices
sections.text: On your first lukio day you choose long or short maths, whether to start a new language, and three or four years. Four years means fewer courses a period: lighter school days, one more year. You can switch until your third year; long maths can become short, not back.

sections.heading: The plan
sections.text: The study counsellor spreads your 75 courses over the periods: every compulsory course, and optional ones in your exam subjects first. The first year is the busiest, and the last spring is kept free for the exams. The School page shows the whole plan.

sections.heading: Each period
sections.text: A stop on a period's first day shows its courses. Move a course to a later period, add an optional one or drop one. In a sports lukio you may also leave out some compulsory courses, never in a subject you take an exam in.

sections.heading: Ask or let the counsellor
sections.text: In the Training tab's standing orders, "Lukio courses" decides whether you look at the courses every period (the default) or the study counsellor plans them and you only get a message. You can always change the plan on the School page.

sections.heading: Grades
sections.text: Each course has its exam in the period's exam week. At the end you get the grades, 4 to 10, as a message, and as a stop only when a course failed. A subject's grade is the average of its courses. A failed course is retaken in the next exam week. Coaching and study counselling are just passed.

sections.heading: Coaching courses
sections.text: At a sports lukio your morning practice counts as 12 coaching courses. They are training, so they don't make school days heavier.

sections.heading: The rules
sections.text: Finnish and at least four more exams, from at least three groups: maths, Swedish, a foreign language and a realia subject such as history or biology. At least one must be a long syllabus, such as long English. All within three sessions in a row.

sections.heading: Planning
sections.text: Your plan says which exam you take in which session: spring (March-April) or autumn (September). The counsellor's suggestion is filled in. Play stops before each session's registration deadline so you can check it; after the deadline that session is fixed.

sections.heading: Exam days
sections.text: Each exam is on its real date, six hours from 9:00, and play stops that morning: sit it or skip it. A skipped exam counts as failed and is retaken at a later session. Exam days are heavy school days.

sections.heading: Grades
sections.text: Results come about two months later: L, E, M, C, B, A or I (failed). Your level in the subject and the optional courses you took in it help most. A failed exam can be retaken. When every exam needed is passed and your courses are done, you graduate.

sections.heading: Moods, not abilities
sections.text: They change week to week. Big news moves them at once: a personal best, a last place, an injury, a goal met, what you answer someone. Every Sunday night each one also settles a little towards where your situation pulls it.

sections.heading: Confidence
sections.text: Low, Shaky, OK, Confident, Flying. Good races, goals met and getting into the school you wanted raise it; races well below your level, last places and a rejected application lower it. At its ends it changes your race time a little, most at big meets.

sections.heading: Motivation
sections.text: Flat, Low, OK, Keen, Fired up. A coach you click with, new things and staying healthy lift it; the same training for months, a long layoff and stress wear it down. It changes how much your sessions train you, never what you do.

sections.heading: Stress
sections.text: Calm, Busy, Stressed, Overwhelmed. A big meet coming, a long injury, training far above your normal and a strained coach raise it, and so does school: a week full of tests, an exam week, a matriculation exam, heavy study, late nights and two practices on a school day. Holidays ease it. It drags motivation down.

sections.heading: The middle does nothing
sections.text: While confidence and motivation say OK and stress says Calm, nothing changes: you train and race as normal. Only the words around them matter.

sections.heading: Your coach
sections.text: In the Sunday talk your coach may mention a mood, and when one is low he asks how you are. A coach good at motivating lifts you more; a good mental coach brings confidence back faster.

sections.heading: The three kinds
sections.text: Imagery: picturing the race before it happens, strongest the week before a target. Relaxation and breathing: lowers stress, and halves the nerves before a big meet. Self-talk: what you tell yourself when it hurts, with a cue word.

sections.heading: Small on purpose
sections.text: Each is one short session a week with no body strain. Together, over a year, they make you about half a point calmer under pressure (composure). Research finds real but modest effects, so don't expect miracles.

sections.heading: Your cue word
sections.text: Pick it with the arrows. It shows on every decision card in your races.

sections.heading: Other ways to grow
sections.text: Consistency grows with every race, more from races unlike your last one. Composure also grows at big meets: national and international ones. A good mental coach helps both.

sections.heading: What they are
sections.text: In general base and spring base, every fourth week of the phase is lighter: every day is one step easier (Hard to Normal, Normal to Easy). The week strip marks turn blue.

sections.heading: Why
sections.text: The body gets stronger in the easier days after hard work. Lighter weeks let it catch up, so you can train more over the season with less risk. You can switch them off per phase.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.text: When a new phase starts, its sessions come in a day at a time over its first weeks, while the rest of the week stays as in the phase before.

sections.heading: Why
sections.text: The first weeks of new hard work, such as the first 800 m intervals of the winter, are when injuries are most likely. A gentle change lets the body get used to it.

sections.heading: Not the same as easing back in
sections.text: Easing in belongs to every new phase. Easing back in is the coach's few easier weeks after a layoff of two weeks or more without running.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.text: After two weeks or more without running, for any reason, your club coach offers two to four easier weeks, longer after a longer break. They sit over your plan, in a season plan and in a repeating week.

sections.heading: How the weeks work
sections.text: Week one: one easy session a day, hard and fast sessions become an easy run. Week two: one session a day at Normal, one hard session kept. A long break ends with a lighter week. Race days stay, with an easy day before.

sections.heading: Where you see it
sections.text: The line over the week strip, the day editor's plan line and the Report show the week you are in. The Training tab has a box with the weeks and Stop easing back in, which returns you to your full plan from today.

sections.heading: Targets ◆
sections.text: The meets your season builds up to, at most three. Your coach picks the main indoor and outdoor championships for you. The first indoor and first outdoor target decide when the phases fall; a third one only gets a taper.

sections.heading: Changing them
sections.text: Add or remove targets in the Training tab, or with Make target in the Calendar. Making a meet a target enters it when you can; withdrawing from it takes it off the list.

sections.heading: The taper
sections.text: The ten days before a target: fewer sessions and no long runs so you arrive fresh, one sharp session three days out to keep your speed, then a rest day and an easy day.

sections.heading: SM limit
sections.text: To enter the Finnish youth championships (Nuorten SM) for 14–15-year-olds you need a time for your age class, or you use your one free event. The limits are the Finnish Athletics Federation's (SUL), from 2026.

sections.heading: Team Finland
sections.text: SUL picks juniors (14–16) and youth (17–21) for its coach groups when they reach a time for their age. The group gives camps and coaching. These times are among the milestones your coach may set.

sections.heading: Kalevan kisat
sections.text: The Finnish senior championships. The limit is the same for every age: 1:53.50 for men and 2:11.00 for women. For a young runner it is a dream for later.

sections.heading: Old tables
sections.text: The tables are SUL's for 2026. New ones come out each February. Until then the game uses the old ones, and a goal built on them says so.

sections.heading: Meets and targets
sections.text: Your coach also suggests a meet to race or a meet to make a target, when he sees a reason: a gap in your racing, a tune-up before a target, a limit within reach. Never more than one a month. He never enters you himself: you say yes or no thanks.

sections.heading: When he does it
sections.text: Only when something catches his eye: sore legs, tired legs, a race close, or a lighter week you asked for in the Sunday talk. At most twice a week. A coach good at load management looks further ahead and sees more truly.

sections.heading: Your setting
sections.text: In Standing orders (Training tab). Ask me first: he sends the change as a message and Play week stops for it. Always, tell me: he changes the day and tells you. Never: he changes nothing, only says what he would have changed.

sections.heading: Veto
sections.text: You decide. Veto keeps your plan, in the message or in the day. Give a reason and it costs nothing. Two silent vetoes in four weeks are fine; after that each one costs a little trust.

sections.heading: Scratching
sections.text: With an injury before a race he may advise you to scratch. He never scratches you himself: he always asks, and on Never he only says so. Ignoring a real warning of his costs a little trust.

sections.heading: What he answers
sections.text: Good idea, Fine, Pointless or Risky, with his reason. He weighs the training you gain or lose, the injury risk and how fresh you will be for your next races.

sections.heading: What he compares
sections.text: A changed day or week against the plan; an unchanged one against an easier version; a race against scratching it. The line under his name says what he compared.

sections.heading: He can be wrong
sections.text: His view is only as good as he is. A coach strong in endurance, speed, load management and planning is nearly always right; a weak one can be wrong both ways. A demanding coach dislikes easy days, a careful one likes them.

sections.heading: Just a question
sections.text: Asking changes nothing and costs nothing, and it is not written into your messages. The same question on the same day gets the same answer.
